analysis.one_liner: Repeals federal sugar price supports and import quotas that keep sugar prices high.
analysis.headline: The bill, which had 5 cosponsors, was referred to the House Agriculture Committee and never received a vote before the 116th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would eliminate the federal sugar program: price-support loans for domestic sugarcane and sugar beet processors, the marketing allotments and tariff-rate quotas that limit how much sugar can be sold and imported at lower tariff rates, and a program that has the USDA buy surplus sugar from processors and resell it to bioenergy producers [S2][S3]. Together these programs keep the supply of sugar in the US market restricted — the price-support mechanism and import quotas are how the program maintains higher domestic sugar prices than would otherwise prevail. Repeal would let more sugar onto the market and remove the government's price floor and purchasing backstop [S2][S3].
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary consumers, who pay more for sugar and sweetened foods than they would in an unrestricted market, and the food and candy manufacturers that use large volumes of sugar as an input [S2].

how_it_helps.text: Eliminates the price-support loan program for domestically grown sugarcane and sugar beet processors, removing the government-backed price floor that supports higher sugar prices [S2][S3].

Repeals the sugar marketing allotments and tariff-rate quotas that limit the quantity of domestically produced sugar processors may sell and the sugar that may be imported under lower tariff rates, easing the supply restrictions that keep domestic prices elevated [S2][S3].

Ends the feedstock flexibility program, under which USDA buys surplus sugar from domestic processors to avoid loan forfeitures and resells it to bioenergy producers — a government backstop for processor revenue [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Domestic sugarcane and sugar beet growers and processors, who would lose their guaranteed prices, sales allotments, protected import limits, and the USDA sugar-purchase backstop; sugar-growing regions could see reduced farm revenue and processing jobs [S2][S3].
analysis.who_pays_short: Sugar beet and cane growers and processors

drawbacks.text: Domestic sugar growers and processors would face competition from unrestricted imports and the loss of guaranteed prices, which supporters of the program argue would shrink US sugar production and cost jobs in sugar-growing districts — the bill's repeal of marketing allotments and tariff-rate quotas directly opens the domestic market to more foreign sugar [S2][S3].

The price-support and marketing-allotment structure is designed so that loans are repaid and forfeitures are avoided; ending the feedstock flexibility program removes the mechanism that prevents government losses on sugar loans, and critics of repeal argue the program costs taxpayers little as currently run [S2][S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is spread thin — a lower price on sugar and sweetened foods for every household — while the cost falls on a concentrated, politically well-organized group of growers and processors concentrated in a few states and districts. That asymmetry is exactly why the program has survived despite the broad consumer cost: a small, focused industry has more to fight for than diffuse consumers do to defend. The bill was a clean repeal with no transition aid for growers, which makes the adjustment sharper for the affected farm regions.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Agriculture Committee and then to a subcommittee, and it never received a markup or a floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Scott Perry introduced the SWEET Act on July 11, 2019, with four Republican cosponsors (Reps. Kelly of Pennsylvania, Joyce of Pennsylvania, and Smucker, plus one Independent), and it was referred to the House Committee on Agriculture [S3][S4][S5].

On August 9, 2019, the bill was referred to the Subcommittee on General Farm Commodities and Risk Management, where it stayed; the Agriculture Committee never advanced it and the full House never voted on it [S5][S1].
The bill died when the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021, without any action beyond referral [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Sugar beet and cane growers and processors kept the price supports, sales allotments, import limits, and USDA purchase backstop that the bill would have repealed — and consumers kept paying the elevated prices the program sustains. The House Agriculture Committee, whose jurisdiction it was, faced no vote on the matter.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Sugar growers, processors, and the committee that shelved it

for.name: Rep. Scott Perry
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to repeal the federal sugar program and sought cosponsors.

for.name: Reps. Mike Kelly (PA), David Joyce (PA), Lloyd Smucker (PA), and one Independent member
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill at introduction, giving it 5 cosponsors total.

against.name: House Committee on Agriculture leadership
against.role: Committee of referral (chair: Rep. Collin Peterson, D-MN)
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to the Subcommittee on General Farm Commodities and Risk Management and never scheduled a markup or advanced it to the House floor.

against.name: Domestic sugar growers and processors
against.role: Beneficiaries of the sugar price-support and import-quota program
against.what_they_did: Defended the sugar program, which they fund-raise and lobby to preserve, and the Agriculture Committee with jurisdiction over it never acted on repeal proposals.

sides.party_line_note: The bill's support was not a party bloc: its 5 cosponsors were 4 of 197 House Republicans plus the chamber's sole Independent; the Agriculture Committee chairman who never scheduled action was a Democrat, and opposition to sugar-program repeal has historically crossed party lines because sugar-producing districts sit in both parties.

industries.industry: Domestic sugarcane and sugar beet growers and processors
industries.note: The bill removes their price-support loans, sales allotments, protected import limits, and the USDA program that buys their surplus sugar — all of which prop up their revenue by keeping domestic sugar prices above what an open market would produce. That industry gain is ordinary consumers' cost.

industries.industry: Sugar-using food and beverage manufacturers (candy, baked goods, cereals)
industries.note: Repeal would lower the price of their main ingredient, cutting costs that are currently passed on to consumers. These manufacturers have long supported sugar-program repeal.
The feedstock flexibility program routes USDA-purchased surplus sugar to bioenergy producers; repeal ends that supply arrangement, though it is a byproduct of ending the broader subsidy structure.
